Take-off and landing times

How OPDI finds the actual take-off time (ATOT) and the actual landing time (ALDT) of a flight, by two methods, and the runway used.

In one sentence

ATOT is the moment the wheels leave the runway and ALDT the moment they touch it, found from the aircraft’s own position reports over the runway, or, where those are missing, from the first reports of the climb or the last reports of the descent.

What it needs

  • The cleaned position reports of the track (one every 5 seconds; see Cleaning of position reports).
  • The departure and destination airports of the flight list, and the other airports close to the start and the end of the track (see Departure and destination airports). Runway events are looked for only at these airports.
  • The runways of the airport from OurAirports, an open database of airports: the position of each end (threshold), the length and the width. The true bearing of a runway is computed from its two thresholds.
  • For the first method: reports on the runway or less than 1 NM short of it. For the second: reports in the first or last 1,500 ft of the flight within 5 NM of the airport.

How it is computed

Two methods give the time. The first, the runway-pass method (written acdm in info.method), follows the aircraft on the runway. The second, the runway-window method (legacy), reads the initial climb or the final descent. The published time comes from the first method when it finds one, and from the second otherwise.

Height above the ground

Both methods need the height of the aircraft above the runway. Aircraft report a barometric altitude, measured from air pressure against the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa. On a day of low or high pressure an aircraft standing on the runway reads several hundred feet above or below the airport’s elevation (from −571 to +232 ft on one measured day). OPDI therefore measures height from the aircraft’s own altitude on the ground:

  1. At each airport the track visits, take its reports at the runways that are flagged on the ground by the transponder, or slower than 30 kt and not climbing or descending faster than 300 ft/min. Airliners send no altitude on the ground, so the reports with an altitude within 30 s of these are read too.
  2. Among their altitudes, take the highest that is at most 30 ft above the lowest (altitudes come in steps of 25 ft). This is the track’s ground altitude at that airport. A track that lands, stands and departs again gets one ground altitude per visit (a silence of more than 300 s starts a new visit).
  3. When the track has no such report, or the result is more than 1,000 ft from the airport’s published elevation, the published elevation is used. info.height_reference says which was used (track or elevation).

Runway-pass method (method = acdm)

  1. Runway grid. Each runway of each large and medium airport is covered with H3 cells of resolution 12 (each about 300 m²). H3 is an open grid that divides the Earth into hexagons. The grid holds the runway itself and, at each end, an approach area reaching 1 NM out from the threshold.
  2. Runway pass. The reports of a track whose cell lies in the grid of one runway, in time order, form a runway pass. A silence of more than 300 s starts a new pass.
  3. Direction of the runway. Each runway has two directions (for example 07 and 25). The direction of a pass is the one within 90° of the aircraft’s median direction of travel over the ground (its ground track), taken over the reports faster than 50 kt. One pass per runway is kept. Of passes of the same kind on parallel runways at overlapping times, the one with reports on its own runway and the smallest median distance from its centre line is kept.
  4. Kind of pass. The pass is a departure when the angle between the ground track and the runway is at most 30°, the highest ground speed is above 50 kt, the height is below 15 ft at the start and at least 15 ft at the end, and the pass ends in the air: neither the report that gives the end height nor the last report of the pass is flagged on the ground. A circuit (take-off and landing on one runway a few minutes apart) is still a departure when the pass holds two reports in the air between 100 and 3,000 ft above the ground. The pass is an arrival under the mirror conditions: angle at most 30°, faster than 50 kt, at least 15 ft at the start and below 15 ft at the end. A pass at an angle between 30° and 45° gives no event: naming no movement is better than naming the wrong one.
  5. ATOT is the moment the height rises through 15 ft, and ALDT the moment it falls through 15 ft. The time and position are interpolated in a straight line between the two reports either side. A dead band of 5 ft on each side (the height must pass from below 10 ft to above 20 ft) keeps a short bounce from giving two times. A report without altitude is skipped; a report with an altitude but no position takes the position interpolated between the positioned reports before and after it when both are within 30 s. When the two reports either side of 15 ft are more than 60 s apart, no time is given (info.bracket_s holds that time).

Runway-window method (method = legacy)

This method follows the runway detection of the traffic library and is used at the departure and destination airports of the flight list only.

  1. Keep the reports within 5 NM of the airport, at most 1,500 ft above its published elevation, faster than 30 kt and climbing (for a departure) or descending (for an arrival) faster than 257 ft/min.
  2. At least 4 reports must remain: they are the initial climb or the final descent.
  3. Runway. The candidate runways are those whose direction is within 10° of the median ground track of these reports; the one whose centre line is nearest to their median position wins.
  4. Only reports at most 0.5 NM from that runway’s extended centre line count. For a landing, a report on the ground (flagged, or slower than 50 kt) must follow when the track continues for more than 120 s.
  5. Time. The take-off time is the time of the earliest of these reports, and the landing time the time of the latest. The event takes that report’s position and altitude. info.at_track_edge is true when the report is the first report of the track (take-off) or its last (landing): reception then started in the climb or ended on final approach.
  6. Height check. The time is kept only when its report is at most 1,500 ft above the track’s ground altitude at the airport, on the same visit (see Height above the ground). Step 1 already keeps only reports at most 1,500 ft above the published elevation, so this check removes a time only when the ground altitude reads below the elevation (on a day of high pressure, because the altitude is measured against standard pressure). Where the ground reads at or above the elevation, or no ground altitude is known, it removes nothing.

One take-off and one landing per track and airport

  1. Each track keeps at most one ATOT and one ALDT at each airport (info.apt_icao): the runway-pass time when there is one (the earliest take-off and the latest landing), otherwise the runway-window time. Two readings of one movement are at one airport and give one event; a track that holds several flights keeps the landing at a stop on the way and the landing at its destination.
  2. The plausibility checks remove an ATOT or ALDT more than 1,500 ft above the ground at its airport. When the height comes from the elevation rather than the track, 1,000 ft is added to that limit for the error of barometric altitude.

Based on

  • Runway-window method: a port of the take-off runway detection of the traffic library (TrackBasedRunwayDetection), with its limits: within 5 NM of the airport, below 1,500 ft, faster than 30 kt, climbing faster than 257 ft/min, at least 4 reports and runways within 10°. traffic detects take-offs only; OPDI applies the mirror rule to landings, measures height above the track’s ground altitude and adds the checks of steps 4 and 6.
  • Runway-pass method: developed for OPDI.
  • Definitions: ATOT and ALDT are the take-off (milestone 16) and landing (milestone 6) of the A-CDM Implementation Manual. The codes T08 and T17 in info.milestone are labels in the PRU flight diagram, not the manual’s numbers; see Milestones of a flight.
  • Related work: Schultz, Rosenow and Olive (2022) derive ATOT and ALDT from ADS-B by the change of the “on the ground” flag, a simpler rule than either OPDI method.
  • Data: runways from OurAirports, runway grid on H3.

What is published

Event types ATOT and ALDT in the flight events file, with position, altitude, distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s. Their info holds apt_icao (airport), runway (direction, for example 25R), runway_bearing_deg and method (acdm or legacy). Times of the runway-pass method also carry traversal_class, align_deg, max_gs_kt, milestone, bracket_s and height_reference; times of the runway-window method carry role, bearing_error_deg, n_samples and at_track_edge. Every field is listed in the Data dictionary.

The flight list repeats them: atot and rwy_dep, rwy_dep_bearing_deg from the earliest ATOT at the departure airport; aldt and rwy_arr, rwy_arr_bearing_deg from the latest ALDT at the destination airport (see Milestone columns of the flight list).

Use cases

  • Taxi-out and taxi-in times per airport: ATOT minus AOBT, and AIBT minus ALDT, of the same flight. Both events must exist, which depends on reception on the ground at the airport.
  • Runway use: count take-offs and landings per runway direction and hour from info.runway, for example to see when an airport changes direction.
  • Time in the air: ALDT minus ATOT. A track that holds several flights has one of each per airport it visits: pair them by info.apt_icao and time.

Limitations

The time is missing when the aircraft was not received near the runway, and runway-window times (legacy) are less precise than runway-pass times (acdm); use info.method to separate them. See Limitations: take-off and landing.

Availability and accuracy

Availability is how often a recorded take-off or landing has an OPDI time; accuracy is how close that time is to the airport’s record.

Three days together (10, 14 and 17 June 2026). “Out of” is the number of flights, records or compared values the share is computed over, to four significant figures.
